newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists, govmt set for Russian spending fight.
newsitem.headline: Communists, govmt set for Russian spending fight.

text.p: Government plans to cut spending across the board to offset dismal Russian tax revenues could open the door to a new row with the lower house of parliament.

Communist Gennady Zyuganov, whose party is the largest group in the State Duma, said on Tuesday the communists would "under no circumstances" back attempts to cut spending and the Duma's communist chairman said such a move would be unpopular.

"Instead of revitalising industry and conducting a normal tax policy, ministers are keeping the old fiscal policy started by (former reform chief Yegor) Gaidar and here they will go bankrupt and break their necks," Zyuganov told Reuters.
Ministers say spending cuts -- known as sequestration -- are the only way to cope with Russia's dismally low tax revenue without busting the budget and throwing reforms off track.

Some officials say plans on sequestration could be presented this month and the head of the Duma's tax committee said even so-called "protected items" could be at risk. These include payments for health, education and the military.
Zyuganov said this should not be allowed to happen.

"The protected items of the budget are called protected because they cannot be touched, especially by crooks like the ones gathered around Chubais today," he said, referring to reformist First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais.

The budget, approved by parliament after prolonged horse-trading and much debate, provides for sequestration if revenues are more than than 10 percent below planned levels, and officials admit this has been the case this year.

President Boris Yeltsin, quoted by Itar-Tass news during a meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, said March revenues were just 42 percent of target, but Chernomyrdin said the figure was provisional and could be changed.
Other officials have put March revenues at 80 percent of targeted levels.
Chernomyrdin or Chubais will brief the Duma on the first quarter budget on April 23.

Chubais, one of several reformists appointed by Yeltsin last month, has promised to kick-start stalled reforms in an effort to revive the economy and win financial backing from the International Monetary Fund.
The IMF has already delayed several loan payments to Russia because of the low tax revenues, although Managing Director Michel Camdessus gave long-term plans a cautious seal of approval last week.
"This country can be an economic superpower, but this cannot be achieved without reforms," Camdessus told the Duma's budget committee.

Analysts said lower spending and a more realistic budget could help Russia out of its lengthy economic slump, provided the new government team held to its ambitious plans to reform and restructure the long-suffering economy.

"If they can manage to hang things together this year and keep inflation under control, one would expect the economy to start to pick up this year," said Vladimir Konovalov, chief economist at the World Bank in Moscow.
"We are hoping that we will start to see some kind of a turnaround."
